Your brain becomes more vulnerable to cognitive decline, your blood vessels stiffen, your liver and kidneys have to work harder to filter toxins, and even your mitochondria (the tiny powerhouses inside your cells) become less efficient at producing energy.

Over time, this inflammatory burden accelerates the aging of your organs, making you feel older than your biological age.

The good news is that inflammation isn't something you simply have to accept.

Through the foods you eat, the way you regulate your blood sugar, prioritize sleep, manage stress, and even how you use fasting strategically, you can create an internal environment that allows your body to repair, regenerate, and age with far more resilience 💙

One of the most powerful markers of long-term health that I encourage everyone to know is their hemoglobin A1C.

It gives you a picture of how well your body has been managing blood sugar over the past few months, and when that number starts to climb, so does your risk for metabolic disease, cognitive decline, heart disease, and a shorter healthspan.

The exciting part is that exercise is one of the fastest ways to improve it.

Every time you challenge your muscles (whether it's walking after a meal, lifting weights, or doing a few sets of squats) those muscles become hungry for glucose, pulling sugar out of your bloodstream without requiring as much insulin.

That's why movement isn't just about burning calories; it's about improving metabolic flexibility and protecting your future.

If your goal is longevity, don't just ask, "How long can I live?" Ask, "How healthy can I keep my metabolism?" Because every workout is an investment in lowering your A1C and giving your body another chance to thrive 💙

The mechanism behind A1C is also its blind spot. Glucose slowly sticks to hemoglobin with no enzyme involved, and since red cells live about three to four months, the glycated fraction becomes a running average of your sugar over that window. The catch is it assumes everyone's red cells live the same length of time. Anything that shortens their lifespan, like recent blood loss or high cell turnover, drags the number falsely low, while longer lived cells push it falsely high. It also averages away swings, so two people with the same A1C can have very different post meal spikes. A strong trend marker, not the whole glucose story. 🔬

It's also about creating moments of safety for your nervous system through sleep, time in nature, breathwork, meaningful connection, and practices like fasting used wisely.

When you calm the stress response, you begin creating the internal environment where both your microbiome (and your metabolism) can finally thrive 💙

caption:
One of the biggest mistakes I see women make when they're trying to lose weight is focusing only on the amount of calories they're eating instead of HOW they're eating it.

Every time you create a large blood sugar spike, you're asking your body to produce more insulin - and insulin is your fat-storage hormone.

If insulin stays elevated all day because you're constantly riding that blood sugar roller coaster, it becomes much harder for your body to access stored fat for fuel. That's why the order of your food matters just as much as the food itself.

When you start a meal with fiber-rich vegetables, healthy fats, or protein before reaching for carbohydrates, you naturally slow the rise in blood sugar and create a gentler insulin response.

Over time, these small shifts improve your metabolic flexibility, reduce cravings, stabilize your energy, and make it much easier for your body to tap into fat stores.

Sustainable weight loss isn't about fearing carbohydrates. It's about creating the right hormonal environment so your body feels safe burning fat instead of storing it 💙

caption:
The Capitol has opened the prediction market for pharmaceutical trials and FDA decisions.

On July 16, Kalshi opened prediction markets on late-stage clinical trials and FDA approval decisions. It built the markets with AppliedXL, a company that monitors and forecasts trial outcomes. By mid-afternoon on day one, Kalshi's medicine market had already moved $128,401.

More than a dozen contracts went live at launch. You can bet on the FDA approving Gilead's experimental cancer drug anito-cel by year's end, or on Summit's lung cancer drug ivonescimab clearing review. There's a contract on whether AriBio's Alzheimer's drug hits the main goals of its late-stage trial, and one on when Eli Lilly's weight loss drug retatrutide gets approved. One contract even asks whether the FDA will approve a cure for Type 1 diabetes before 2033, and more than four in ten bettors said yes. 

Kalshi did build some guardrails. Nothing gets listed until a trial has finished enrolling patients and every contract is tied to a single public document that settles it, like the primary endpoint registered on ClinicalTrials.gov or the FDA's approval letter. Additionally, AppliedXL writes the rule for how to read that document before trading opens, so nobody's reinterpreting it once the results are in. And traders have to verify their employment, and anyone sitting on material nonpublic information is barred.

Researchers who study trials aren't reassured. They told STAT News that once money is riding on an outcome, anyone with influence over a study has a reason to alter or delay decisions. The bigger worry is what it does to science itself. When there's a market to move, getting the evidence right stops being the only thing driving decisions. Patients might stay enrolled or drop out based on the public odds instead of their clinician's advice. And the people best positioned to profit are the ones who see the data first, including company staff and the clinicians running the study.

caption:
Menopause is so much more than the end of your reproductive years, it's one of the greatest neurological and emotional recalibrations you'll ever experience.

For decades, estrogen has influenced not only your metabolism and your cells, but also your brain, your mood, your resilience, and even the way you perceive the world around you.

As estrogen begins to decline, many women find themselves looking at their relationships, careers, habits, and priorities through an entirely different lens.

You may suddenly question dynamics you've tolerated for years or feel a deep pull toward a life that feels more authentic. This isn't because you're becoming someone new, it's because the hormonal chemistry that once shaped your perspective is changing.

While these fluctuations can feel unsettling, they also create an incredible opportunity.

Menopause invites you to pause, listen to your inner wisdom, and intentionally rebuild your life in a way that honors the woman you're becoming, not just the woman you've always been 💙

caption:
Today, CDC’s ACIP is meeting to discuss the childhood vaccine schedule. We thought it would be a good time to remind everyone just how amazing vaccines are...

What did these diseases look like before vaccines — and what do they look like now?

For the “before” numbers, we used the average annual U.S. cases over the 3–5 years preceding each vaccine introduction. Before vaccines, these diseases didn’t just circulate... they erupted in huge, erratic waves. Some years were “quiet,” and others brought explosive epidemics. Using a multi-year average gives a realistic picture of the true, constant threat families faced.

For the “now,” we used the most recent finalized CDC counts. Thanks to vaccines, modern case numbers have been remarkably stable and dramatically lower — a level of predictability and protection that simply didn’t exist before immunization. (Though we’re now seeing cracks where vaccination rates decline.)

FYI This was inspired by a smart, clear graphic from the Public Health Agency of Canada — so we created a U.S. version.

TL;DR: Diseases that once infected hundreds of thousands — or even millions — of Americans every year have fallen by more than 90–99%. That’s public health. ❤️

One of the reasons so many people feel like they're constantly battling hunger is because their body isn't getting the signals it needs to naturally produce enough GLP-1.

This incredible hormone isn't something your body just turns on automatically, it responds to the information you're giving it every time you eat. And one of the most powerful signals you can send is fiber.

Fiber-rich foods feed your gut microbiome, slow digestion, and stimulate specialized cells in your intestines that help release GLP-1.

When your meals are filled with processed, fiber-poor foods, those signals become weaker, and it's much harder for your body to create the feelings of fullness and satisfaction you're looking for.

That's why I encourage women to stop chasing the next weight loss hack and start asking, "How do I help my body do what it already knows how to do?"

The answer often starts with colorful vegetables, legumes, seeds, berries, and other whole, fiber-rich foods that nourish your gut and remind your body to turn on its own powerful appetite-regulating hormones 🙌

The part that makes this practical is where the machinery actually sits. GLP-1 comes from L cells packed into the far end of the small intestine and the colon, not the stomach, so anything meant to trigger them has to still be intact by the time it arrives down there. That is the logic behind the ileal brake, and it is why intact protein and fat move that signal more than something fully absorbed in the first stretch of gut. The kinetics matter just as much. Your own GLP-1 gets broken down by an enzyme called DPP-4 within roughly two minutes of release, so the body was never built around one big surge. It runs on repeated modest signaling across a meal, which is a very different target than chasing a spike 🔬

The variability piece is what makes this more than a scale story. Two people can share the same average glucose and A1C while one rides sharp spikes and crashes all day, and it's the amplitude of those swings that does much of the damage, driving oxidative stress and endothelial strain more than a steady, modestly higher number does. caption:
Like any medication that changes your body's biology, we have to be willing to have an honest conversation about both the benefits AND the risks of GLP-1s.

One of the concerns I have is the amount of muscle many people lose while taking these medications.

Some of that happens because rapid weight loss naturally includes some lean mass, but it can be made worse when people aren't eating enough protein, aren't strength training, or simply aren't consuming enough overall nutrition because their appetite is so suppressed.

Muscle is your metabolic engine.

It supports blood sugar balance, insulin sensitivity, longevity, and healthy aging. And when your nutrition suffers over time, it's not just your muscles that pay the price.

Your bones depend on adequate protein, minerals, and mechanical stress from movement to stay strong.

If we're reducing food intake without intentionally protecting muscle and bone health, we risk trading short-term weight loss for long-term metabolic resilience. That's why I believe the conversation around GLP-1s has to include a strategy for preserving the very tissues that help us stay healthy, strong, and independent for decades to come 💙

What I struggle with is when the conversation becomes all-or-nothing. Population-level evidence tells us about trends and system effects, but it doesn’t erase the ethical dilemma faced by the individual woman who has been suffering for months or years without access to care. It also doesn’t erase the reality of clinicians who have reached a point where working in the public system is no longer sustainable.

I think compassion has to remain part of this conversation. When people become desperate enough to pay hundreds of dollars out of pocket, I’m less interested in judging that choice and more interested in asking why our system left them feeling they had no reasonable alternative in the first place.

We should also hold accountable clinics or clinicians who exploit those gaps. But I don’t think blaming individual patients or assuming every clinician working privately is simply “spinning a story” moves us closer to that goal.

To me, this isn’t about choosing between public or private care. It’s about recognizing that both things can be true: private care may have unintended consequences for the public system, and asking people to continue suffering while they wait for systemic change is an ethical cost we shouldn’t ignore.

caption:
You get a flu vaccine every year, but you may never need another MMR vaccine in your life. Two vaccines, completely different schedules, and that one gap explains most of what trips people up about adult vaccines.

Two different things decide whether you’re due for another vaccine dose. Sometimes the germ keeps changing and the vaccine has to keep up, which is the story with flu and COVID vaccines and why they get updated every year. Other times your protection slowly fades and needs a top-up, which is why a tetanus booster shot comes back around every ten years. Some vaccines, such as MMR, which protects against measles, mumps, and rubella, tend to provide lifelong protection once the recommended doses are complete. People at higher risk, such as healthcare workers or international travelers, may need a second dose.

We also answer other questions that come up often, such as whether grandparents need a Tdap before meeting a new baby, and what to do if you’re over 40 and can’t track down your childhood records. 

Note that we are writing a standalone post on adult vaccines to prepare for a newborn, so stay tuned!

caption:
I have a lot of new followers so I want to de-up this post about how much money doctors can make selling supplements. The fact that many of these supplements are promoted based on cherry picking the literature is a separate issue. This post from TheVajenda.com is about the cash grab. 

I went through the process of creating my own turmeric supplement to show you just how much money a doctor can make. For every bottle I sell at $35, I make a $24.93 profit. If I sell 8,333 bottles of turmeric, my profit is $195,000. 

If you want to take a supplement physician brands are not better than NatureMade or any other less expensive product. If you are taking a supplement, look for one with a third party verification ON THE LABEL. 

Also, ACOG advises against physicians selling supplements. It creates a history of of ethical issues. This is from the ACOG Opinion statement: 

Obstetrician–gynecologists should not use their professional influence or clinical environment to sell or promote nonmedical products or services or to enroll participants into multilevel marketing schemes.

caption:
Dr. Libby Weaver coined the term Rushing Woman's Syndrome to describe something so many women are living every single day - not a medical diagnosis, but a pattern of constant urgency that keeps the body stuck in survival mode.

We have created a world where being busy has become a badge of honor, and somewhere along the way we forgot that the female body was never designed to be in a perpetual state of "go."

When your nervous system is constantly interpreting deadlines, notifications, overflowing to-do lists, and self-imposed pressure as threats, your biology responds as if you're in danger.

Your body shifts away from rest, repair, digestion, hormone production, and fat burning, and instead prioritizes stress hormones like adrenaline and cortisol.

Before long, you feel tired but wired, your sleep suffers, your cravings increase, your hormones become more chaotic, and your metabolism becomes less resilient.

I believe one of the greatest acts of healing available to women today isn't finding another supplement or another diet, it's creating enough moments of safety that your nervous system remembers it no longer has to survive.

That's when your biology can finally do what it was designed to do: heal 🙌

⏯️ Clip from my conversation with @richroll

I wrote about the two new diagnostic tests that for endometriosis that will likely be introduced in the United Kingdom.

These tests have been called game changers by the media and some influencers, but we just don’t have the data to say that. Endotest has been validated outside of its original study, but Endosure has not. The biggest issue with these tests is that they’ve only been tested in populations with very high prevalence of endometriosis and a test really needs to be studied in the population who is going to get that test. So we need data to see how they’ll perform in a real world situation. Hopefully the necessary data will be collected. If they continue to perform as well as their preliminary studies then they would be game changers. The problem is many tests don’t when they make it into the real world. My stance is cautious optimism.

The U.S. spends more on health care than other high-income nations. This isn’t new. But, there are consequences to rising health care costs.

National health spending has grown from 7% of GDP in 1971 to 18% today. Warnings about unsustainable costs go back just as far, from Nixon to Clinton to Obama.

Total national health expenditures reached $5.3 trillion a year in 2024, and recently released government estimates show it going even higher in 2025. As health spending continues to climb, it crowds out other budget priorities for federal, state, and local governments. 

And, rising premiums are straining employers and workers alike. Average annual family premiums for employer coverage have climbed to nearly $27,000, and for individuals, unaffordable care can mean medical debt, delayed care, and financial strain.

Bringing down underlying costs may be central to the next big health care debate. Swipe for more about the macro issues driving U.S. health spending: how we got here — and who pays.

caption:
If you're struggling to fall asleep, waking up at 2 or 3 a.m., or getting a full night's sleep but still feeling exhausted when you wake up, your blood sugar could be part of the story.

When blood sugar drops too low overnight, your brain sees it as an emergency and calls on stress hormones like adrenaline (and cortisol) to bring your blood sugar back up.

That adrenaline surge is often what jolts you awake, leaves your mind racing, or makes it impossible to get back to sleep. And even if you don't fully wake up, those repeated stress responses can keep you from getting the deep, restorative sleep your body needs.

Stable blood sugar doesn't just support your metabolism. It helps your nervous system feel safe enough to stay asleep, repair, regulate hormones, and wake up with real energy instead of relying on caffeine to get through the day 🙌

caption:
Let’s talk about booster shots, and why not every vaccine needs another dose.

Some vaccines provide protection that fades over time and require additional doses to maintain that protection. For example, tetanus and diphtheria protection declines over time, so adults need a Td or Tdap booster dose about every 10 years. Tdap is also recommended in every pregnancy so your baby has some protection against pertussis before they’re born. Measles is a different story. Once you’ve had the recommended doses, you’re covered for life. Flu and COVID vaccines aren’t exactly booster shots. They get updated each season to match what’s circulating, which is why they come around every year.

We’re getting into the details in a carousel coming soon, so stay tuned! Until then, ask your doctor what you’re due for.

caption:
We do not have a randomized double blinded placebo controlled trial that proves the testosterone helps women recover faster after hip fracture. What we have is the  STEP-HI trial, which used doses of testosterone higher than we use for libido. The study did not meet its primary and point which means that testosterone plus an exercise program fared no better than a placebo gel and an exercise program.

it seems that all of the claims online are  based on secondary and post hoc analyses, where two small signals were observed. These two findings are best understood as exploratory. Elevating weak signals from secondary or post hoc analyses to the level of primary evidence can mislead people into thinking they have a new therapy, when what they have is a new hypothesis for future research. 

I wrote another post for TheVajenda.com explaining the study and in the post I have a video from Professor Sue Davis also explaining the findings.  She gave us a fantastic lecture at the Menopause Society meeting last year where she  discussed this particular trial so she graciously repeated that for me to share with you. Please head to TheVajenda.com for the video and post.

Most wellness peptides have little to no human data and, in some cases, lack preclinical studies too.

caption:
The U.S. military just announced it'll screen all service members aged 30 and up for testosterone deficiency, with hormone therapy offered to anyone who tests low. Sounds proactive. The evidence says it's more complicated.

Testosterone naturally declines with age, and "low T" by a blood-test cutoff is common. But how common depends entirely on where you draw the line. Individual study estimates have ranged from as low as 2% to as high as 77%. That variability is the whole problem. 

However, a low number isn't a diagnosis. Actual deficiency (hypogonadism) means consistently low levels and symptoms to match. When you require both, the prevalence drops to roughly 2% overall, rising with age. That's why every major medical society, including the Endocrine Society and the American Urological Association, recommends against screening men who don't have symptoms. Screen large groups of healthy people and you mostly find "abnormal" values that were never going to cause harm, which fuels overdiagnosis and puts people on lifelong therapy they may not need.

None of this means testosterone therapy is bad. For men with a confirmed deficiency, the data show clear benefits. But TRT can also cause infertility, a serious concern for younger troops. It can thicken the blood and affect clotting factors, raising the risk of blood clots, which is why hematocrit is monitored during treatment. And while the 2023 TRAVERSE trial was reassuring on major heart events, it still flagged higher rates of atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism, and kidney injury.

The timing matters too. U.S. regulators have been loosening TRT labeling in stages: the FDA dropped its cardiovascular boxed warning in 2025, and in June 2026 requested (but hasn't finalized) dropping the remaining caution that safety and effectiveness in age-related low T aren't established. More people screened, fewer guardrails, and "High T" branding are how normal aging becomes something to be medicated.

The guidelines are clear on this: test men with symptoms, not everyone who meets an age cutoff. Then have an honest conversation about risks and benefits.

caption:
My latest CIDRAP op-ed is up, and it's about something that really grinds my gears... the idea that death is the only bad thing that can happen if you get measles.

We hear this all the time: "....but the case fatality rate is only one or two in a thousand," as if measles is a coin flip, heads you live, tails you die, nothing in between.

The in-between does a lot of damage. For one, immune amnesia that wipes out part of your immune memory and takes years to rebuild. There's also hospitalizations, airway swelling that lands little kids in the ICU, encephalitis, and SSPE, which can surface years after recovery and is almost always fatal. None of those things show up in a case fatality rate.

The MMR shot protects against all of it, not just the worst case. Read more in the full op-ed over at CIDRAP: https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/measles/cidrap-op-ed-measles-isnt-coin-flip-death-isnt-only-bad-outcome

caption:
An update on the cyclospora front!

For weeks the signal pointed at lettuce and salad greens without a source attached-- now investigators reportedly have one. Shredded iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms, served at some Taco Bell locations, has been identified as a likely source. The FDA is expected to advise people shortly to avoid shredded lettuce at Taco Bell in Michigan, Ohio, West Virginia, Kentucky, and Indiana.

This is still coming from people close to the investigation, and Taco Bell says officials haven't formally confirmed a link to the chain or any supplier. 

Nationally, close to 7,000 people may have been sickened since May 1. About 1,645 of those are confirmed, the rest are still under investigation, and no deaths have been reported. Michigan has been hit hardest by a wide margin and cases could keep rising through the end of August.

What does this mean for you?
If you ate at Taco Bell recently and you've had watery diarrhea, cramping, or bloating that won't let up, check in with your doctor. Cyclospora is treatable with a specific antibiotic once diagnosed. It can stretch on for weeks and come back if you leave it alone.

NOTE: This isn't only a Taco Bell story! Taylor Farms supplies plenty of grocery stores and restaurants, so the broader caution around lettuce and salad greens still holds.

Heat is still the most reliable way to kill this parasite, but that's unlikely to apply to iceberg lettuce, since it's not something you're going to cook. Washing, vinegar soaks, and salad spinners won't dependably get it off produce either. So for the food actually in question here, there's no prep trick that saves it. The safe play is skipping it until this settles out. Heat still earns its place for the other produce cyclospora travels on, like berries or herbs, if you'd rather cook those down than toss them.

If you're pregnant or immunocompromised, it's worth being extra careful right now.

Cyclospora doesn't spread person to person, and symptoms can show up a week or two after exposure. So the cases we're seeing now trace back to exposures from a while ago, and the picture should keep sharpening as investigators pin down the source.

caption:
Peptides. Peptides! PEPTIDES!!

It seems like everywhere you look, a new wellness peptide is going viral as a cure for everything from “cellular regeneration” to “improved mitochondrial function.” Someone in your fitness group swears they started a peptide and feels amazing. And you’re thinking, “Geez, GLP-1s are peptides and have changed people’s lives. Maybe I should try out this other peptide.”

Before trying out that peptide you’ve seen making the rounds on social media, a few things to know: 

- Not all peptides are created equal. Prescription peptide medications like GLP-1 agonists have gone through rigorous scientific development and regulatory approval for human use.

- Wellness peptides are a different story. Many were developed as research tools, never intended for human use. And some were abandoned during development as potential therapeutics because early research raised safety concerns or showed little benefit. 

- There is very little, if ANY, human data supporting the use of many wellness peptides. We’re not saying they don’t work. We simply don’t have the data to know.

- The wellness industry is making BANK on influencer marketing and unregulated wellness peptides, and it’s investing heavily to make sure that you hear about them. 

And there is so much more to this story. Why isn’t pharma working on these peptides? Why do regulations differ between wellness peptides and prescription peptide medications? All of this and more about this peptide craze is coming up in our next post, Peptides Part 2. Stay tuned!

caption:
Summer means more time outside, and more water leaving your body through sweat than you'd guess. Losing just 2% of your body weight in fluid is enough to make it harder for your body to cool down. It can also cloud your thinking and leave you feeling wiped out, often before you notice any thirst.

Kids and older adults are the most vulnerable. Their bodies are slower to regulate temperature and slower to register the need for water. Plenty of older adults don't feel thirsty even when they need to drink. Young children often stop drinking too soon and rely on the adults around them to keep offering fluids. Infants can't ask at all.

For both groups, dehydration can escalate quickly, from mild to heat exhaustion or heat stroke, with extra strain on the kidneys and heart along the way. In older adults, even mild dehydration is linked to worse recoveries in the hospital.

The good news is that this is largely preventable. Offer water often and put out water-rich foods. And check on the people who can't easily ask for a drink, especially during the hottest stretch of the day, roughly 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Swipe through for the signs to watch for and simple ways to help the people you love stay hydrated this summer.

caption:
For decades, women have been told that weight loss is nothing more than a math equation: eat fewer calories, move more, and the weight will come off.

But if it were really that simple, we wouldn't have millions of women feeling more exhausted, more inflamed, and more frustrated than ever before.

The problem with constantly eating less is that it often becomes a slippery slope into chronic restriction, where you're no longer nourishing your body - you're simply trying to outsmart it. And your biology is incredibly intelligent.

When your body senses it's not getting enough fuel, it doesn't necessarily become a better fat burner; it often becomes more protective.

Cortisol rises as your body perceives stress, blood sugar becomes less stable, and over time that hormonal environment can contribute to insulin resistance, making weight loss feel even harder.

That's why I believe sustainable weight loss isn't built on deprivation, it's built on nourishment.

It's eating enough of the right foods to support your hormones, your muscles, and your metabolism, while also giving your digestive system intentional periods of rest through tools like fasting.

Those windows without food allow your body to repair, reset, and become metabolically flexible again. Lasting health doesn't come from eating as little as possible. It comes from learning when to nourish your body deeply and when to step back and allow it the time and space to heal 💙

A newly published review paper in Nature Immunology (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42174266/) offers insights into how our immune system is programmed for lifelong protection. 

Rather than simply “switching on” at birth, research reveals that our immune education begins early in development within the womb. Maternal microbial signals crossing the placenta help “tune” and teach tolerance to the developing immune system before birth. This prenatal training, combined with the critical postnatal influences of birth, breastfeeding, and environmental exposures, ultimately establishes the foundation for how we respond to infections, vaccines (work with the immune system to train to defend), and allergies throughout our entire lives.

Swipe through to explore the science behind how our first experiences shape immunity throughout our lifetime.

caption:
This is a Guest post from @jonathankulpa, a Biomedical Engineer who brought us this analysis.

We’re building health technology capable of tracking heart rate, sleep, activity, blood pressure, fall risk, and more in real time. But the people who could benefit the most from these tools are often the least likely to use them.

This is “The Grey Gap”, the growing divide between the people digital health technology could help the most, and the people most likely to use it.

Using data from the 2024 Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS), the author conducted a secondary analysis on a cleaned subset of 6,665 responses drawn from the original pool of 7,278 survey responses, examining adoption of wearables, health apps, and telehealth across age groups:

Half of adults under 50 reported using wearables, compared to less than 20% of adults 75+.

Adults over 75 had the lowest wearable retention rates after trying the technology.

8% of adults over 75 lacked access to a device entirely.

Where access wasn’t an issue, digital self-perception and finances emerged as the two strongest barriers to adoption.

These findings point to something deeper than usability alone: cost and self-sufficiency with regards to tech may be just as important as interface design.

The future of health tech goes beyond standard accessible design. It may involve technology that disappears into the background entirely, asking less of the user, or even nothing at all.

caption:
🥬Wanted to clear up one thing from yesterday, since a bunch of you had follow up questions about something in our post on food safety during the Cyclospora outbreak.

🧊A lot of you pointed out that freezing doesn't kill the parasite, and you're right, it doesn't. But any affected food is HIGHLY unlikely to be on shelves yet. Frozen produce typically has a long processing lead time, so what's on shelves now was very likely packaged well before this outbreak began. Plus,  the main produce under investigation, lettuce, isn't really sold frozen anyway.

Now, where things stand more broadly: this outbreak is really clustered in the Midwest. Michigan and Ohio are getting hit hardest, and the CDC is tracking a linked cluster across those two plus West Virginia and Kentucky. If you live outside those states, your risk appears to be low, about the same everyday foodborne risk that's always around. There are cases popping up elsewhere, but they don't seem connected to this outbreak. They look like the normal background cases we tend to see this time of year.

Until the specific source is confirmed though (fingers crossed it's soon), it's not a bad idea to err on the side of caution if you're outside those states, especially if you're pregnant or immunocompromised!

Once the source is identified, any potentially impacted products would never make it onto shelves. 

Worth noting too: past Cyclospora outbreaks have consistently been tied to fresh produce, not frozen. 

Please remember that HEAT is the most effective way to kill the parasite, so if you have any concern, heating foods to an internal temp of 158°F (70°C) is your best bet.

Hope this helps clarify!

caption:
A bill with bipartisan support was just introduced, and we are very happy about it. It would modernize the program that compensates people in the rare cases when a vaccine causes a serious injury, and it would finally bring COVID-19 vaccine claims into that system.

A bit about how this works. The Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) has been around since 1986. It's a no-fault system, which means people don't have to sue a manufacturer or prove negligence to be compensated. It runs on a small excise tax on vaccines rather than taxpayer dollars, and it uses an "injury table" that lists injuries known to be associated with certain vaccines. If someone experiences one of those recognized injuries in the expected timeframe, it's presumed connected, and they don't have to prove causation from scratch. Other claims can still be considered, they just require more evidence.

If you're wondering why COVID-19 wasn't already included, it comes down to timing. When the vaccines first rolled out under emergency use authorization, injury claims were routed into a separate, more limited program called the Countermeasures Injury Compensation Program (CICP), which was built for public health emergencies. That program doesn't allow you to appeal a decision, doesn't cover pain and suffering, and has a large backlog of claims that have been sitting without a decision for years. Even after the COVID-19 vaccines received full FDA approval and were added to the immunization schedule, those claims were never moved into the stronger, fairer VICP that covers other routine vaccines. This bill fixes that.

Our support for vaccines has always been about public health, not pharma companies. Vaccines save millions of lives. In the rare instances where someone is injured, we feel strongly that they deserve a fair, timely, and compassionate path to compensation. Standing up for those people and standing up for vaccines are the same thing, and it's encouraging to see both parties recognize that.

We will share updates as we have them.

https://doggett.house.gov/media/press-releases/new-bipartisan-legislation-modernize-vaccine-injury-compensation-provide

caption:
I wasn't sure if I'd missed the boat on weighing in about the Fauci hearing. A lot has been written this week (a lot of it good!), and I didn't want to just repeat it. So, I spent a few days going back through the 2020 record instead of the 2026 coverage...

Watching Wednesday, what struck me is how differently we all remember the same years. If you lost a business or a year of your kid's schooling, the restrictions are what you remember, with the death toll as background. If you were in a hospital that spring, you remember refrigerated trucks and makeshift morgues and bodies on the floor, and the restrictions barely register. Both are accurate accounts of different pieces of the same event.

That's part of why going back to the tape was useful. Some of what people are saying now doesn't line up with what was said at the time. Dr. Fauci was on national television throughout the spring of 2020 talking openly about the tradeoffs of mitigation measures, the potential harms of staying closed too long, and the pushback he was getting from both directions. How that guidance got translated into practice, by governors and school boards and employers, is a different question, and one I don't try to settle.

What people want is a clean verdict on whether all of it was necessary, and for as long as it lasted. That's the part the data can't settle, because the costs all have a face attached and the deaths that didn't happen can't be definitively calculated.

I get into the masks, the lockdown comparisons, COVID's origins, and the misinformation that got a Senate platform on Wednesday.

This topic elicits VERY strong emotions on all sides, and I know some of you will disagree with parts of this. It's long, but I'd ask you to read the whole thing before you decide I got it wrong.

🔗Link in stories, or you can Google 'Unbiased Science Substack' and it'll be the latest article on our page!

Over 25% of U.S. adults over 40 take a statin, whether it be atorvastatin (Lipitor), simvastatin (Zocor), rosuvastatin (Crestor), or others. 

Statins are well-tolerated with a strong safety record. They work primarily by lowering bad cholesterol levels. And in doing so, they reduce the risk of serious heart-related events like heart attack and stroke. 

But statins aren’t without controversy. Questions about their real-world benefits and side effects have fueled ongoing public debate. And the conversation got more complicated in 2012 when the FDA added information about reversible memory loss and confusion to statin labels as possible side effects. That made headlines, and prompted researchers to dig deeper into whether statins cause dementia. 

Spoiler alert: The available research doesn’t show that statins cause dementia. Importantly, the brain produces most of its own cholesterol independently of the bloodstream, so lowering bad cholesterol doesn't simply "deprive the brain" of the cholesterol it needs. Some observational studies have even linked statin use to a lower risk of dementia, but association doesn’t prove causation. Read on to learn what the evidence really shows.

This claim that that the WHO has classified birth control pills as a type 1 carcinogen is misleading and rage bait. I would block any account spreading this. It is a misleading claim that has been around for 20 years and it recirculates every few months. 

When you see a scary claim about the pill, blocking is usually in order because people who care about your health don’t lead with amped up fear. Then check laterally, meaning move off social media and type the claim in your browser with the words “fact check” or “Dr. Jen Gunter Vajenda.” (I’ve written about a lot of rage bait). 

This wasn’t news in 2005 and so it is not news today. 

The classification system from the WHO is not about the severity of the claim, but the strength of the medical evidence behind the claim and those are different things. The WHO also says that ultraviolet rays from the sun are a group 1 carcinogen. 

We weigh medications on their net benefits and negatives. The pill is associated with a very small increased risk in breast cancer. Ribs also associated with a reduced risk of endometrial and ovarian cancer, les iron deficiency, can treat many kinds of pelvic pain, treat heavy bleeding, help manage perimenopause, and of course provide contraception.  But that doesn’t get clicks. 

Also, none of these accounts seem to care about the risk of breast cancer during pregnancy. 

Help build the social media platform you want and block rage bait. It is misogyny dressed up as advocacy.

Welcome to our 3-part series on the 🇨🇦Canada Health Act 🇨🇦 and what it means for your menopause care.

We created this series to help you better understand your healthcare options so you can navigate the system with confidence.

Over the next three posts, we’ll break down what the Canada Health Act actually says about menopause, look at whether private care truly improves access or just makes it worse, and share how you can actually find the menopause support you need right within Canada's public system.

Whether you’re accessing care through the public system or a private clinic, by choice or by circumstance, there is absolutely no judgment. We know people are doing the best they can to get the care they need.

Our goal is simply to ensure you understand what you can access, what questions to ask, and how the Canada Health Act applies to menopause care in Canada.

years experience. I strongly support publicly funded, accessible menopause care and agree that no woman should have to pay privately for basic evidence-based treatment. But saying private care “does not improve access” erases women whose public options are refusal, inadequate care or a two-year wait.
A colleague of mine was denied hormone therapy solely because her mother had breast cancer—a family history that warrants individualized risk assessment, not an automatic prohibition. She obtained an evidence-based private medical consultation, started appropriate treatment and experienced a profound improvement in her quality of life. Another friend suffered for ten years after receiving the same blanket refusal.
We should demand better publicly funded care while refusing to shame women who cannot sacrifice years of their health waiting for the system to improve. Please distinguish exploitative private hormone businesses from regulated clinicians filling a care vacuum. Women seeking timely care did not create this broken system. caption:
Several people have messaged me today about a video from Dr. Zelovitzky (screenshots above) believing that she is referencing my measured videos about how private menopause care in Canada is capitalizing on the gaps in the system and worsening care for those who cannot afford it. I would not fault anyone for drawing that conclusion as Dr. Zelovitsky has previously targeted me. I want to be clear that I blocked her and contacted her employer after she posting this misinformation in a reply to a video about me in February:

“I don’t think she actually sees patients at all anymore. I think her full-time job is just being mean now? I’m also pretty sure she doesn’t give her books or talks or substack articles away for free, so I guess you can be for-profit, but only if it’s the right type of goods you’re selling.”

I had never met her or even heard of her before so this vitriol was surprising, but I admit my content probably touches some financial and marketing nerves. Let’s be clear, anyone with access to Google can see where I practice, so it always shocks me when doctors or NPs can’t figure that out. If she had read my Substack, she would know that 90% or so of the articles are free, all my books are available in libraries, and my show Jensplaining, which has a menopause episode, is free to all in Canada.

Dr. Zelovitsky mentions in her video that she could not “keep the doors open” doing menopause care. The dismal reimbursement was EXACTLY my point. We are in agreement. And let’s be clear, there are many doctors/NPs in Canada doing amazing menopause care inside the Canadian Health Care System and accepting the $32 they get. It’s not right, hence the need for transparency. 

I do not believe the public knows how poorly menopause care is reimbursed and how that shapes training and the structure of the system. Provincial health plans, reward acute care and procedures, while menopause care is largely longitudinal and has been neglected in the coding due to misogyny.

Each province could fix this. It is a choice not to, and private clinics make it easier for them to look away as women with disposable income are getting care.

caption:
Private clinics taking pressure off public healthcare — sounds reasonable, right? But the data tells a different story.
Welcome to Part 2 of our Canada Health Act series on menopause care. 🇨🇦

Here's what's actually happening when care moves private:

Staff shortages worsen: private clinics draw specialized providers away from the public system. Costs of outsourced procedures have increased by 52%, while surgical activity in public hospitals has declined.

The burden shifts — public hospitals are left managing the most complex cases with fewer resources, meaning longer waits for everyone

For menopause care specifically, this widens gaps for the women who already face the most barriers — those in rural communities, lower-income patients, and racialized women who have historically been underserved.  And it reduces the pressure on governments to invest in the public infrastructure we all need.

This is not about judgment if you've gone private. You did what you had to do to get care. But it is important for you to understand the landscape, so you can advocate for yourself and for something better.

Part 3 is coming: how to find menopause support within the public system, and how we can push for change together. 💜

Thank you @danraaza @cdndrs4medicare

#MenopauseCare #CanadaHealth #PublicHealthcare #PatientAdvocacy #WomensHealthCanada HealthPolicy

It's not your fault and getting rid of it is not as simple as "eating less and moving more". 80% of women with PCOS (PMOS) have Insulin resistance which causes more fat to be stored in our midsection! Losing weight with PCOS can be challenging because without managing Insulin Resistance, we get stuck in an endless cycle of symptoms which prevent us from losing the belly fat! 

So what can you do? Here are 3 easy steps to start: 

🏋️‍♀️Slow weighted workouts 3x per week 
🚶🏻‍♀️Walking after meals. 
💊Add supplements like Inositol & Berberine

I had a conversation with Dr. Nanette Santoro, on of the titans of menopause, over at TheVajenda. She has an encyclopedic knowledge of all things menopause from her decades of research and clinical care. We had a wide ranging conversation. Here is an excerpt about estradiol levels. 

All of the top experts who know the literature and who see patients tell us that estradiol levels for managing MHT is misleading. Hope you enjoy the full conversation! I certainly did.

Where can we find the full conversation?
So what do we do ?

As someone with POI and a rare vascular disease on a suboptimal estradiol dose (MHT vs HRT dose), my repro endocrinologist wants to get my estradiol as a data point to discuss increasing to what should be my baseline level with my cardiologist. She said to get it drawn about 48 hours after changing my patch.

I totally agree with this however, I tell my patient when to go for bloodwork in regard to their dosing. I can still better manage dosing by seeing levels and symptom relief. The other reason I look at levels is to measure metabolites.  I would love to have a discussion on the relevance of Estrone to Estradiol ratios and hormonal delivery systems.  Let’s connect. 🙏🏻 I feel metabolites of the hormones we give are the missing link to hormonal safety!
Yes perfect explanation!

This was truly special. Having Dr. Santoro, someone who is so incredibly busy and rarely available, join you for this conversation was nothing short of remarkable. Two world-class references in one place, sharing so much knowledge and wisdom. Thank you for making this happen for all of us! 🙏

caption:
Slow and steady wins the race! 🐢✨

I’ve been on my post partum weight loss journey for 4 months now and honestly… it’s been frustrating! I never expected to have gained so much while pregnant. I gained 70lbs and have 29lbs left to go, but I am SO proud of the progress I’ve made so far! 🤩

I’ve had to really be consistent with all the things that I did in the past to lose weight with PCOS (PMOS): Gluten & Dairy free, slow weighted workouts, prioritizing protein, the right supplements, and everything I talk about here and it’s working! If you are on your post-partum weight loss journey, just know you’re not alone and we’ve got this! 👯‍♀️
